what: some asks: is there at least one element that passes the test? every asks: do all elements pass?
Both stop early. some stops at the first pass (the answer is already yes). every stops at the first fail (the answer is already no).
On an empty array, some is false (nobody passed) and every is true (nobody failed). Think of a teacher asking "did anyone fail?" in an empty class: no.

steps: Check that the callback is a function; otherwise throw a TypeError.
Loop over the indexes from 0 to length - 1, skipping holes (i in arr is false for a hole).
Call cb.call(thisArg, element, index, array).
some: return true on the first truthy result. every: return false on the first falsy result.
After the loop: some returns false, every returns true.

  i=0  3 > 2 ? yes
  i=1  8 > 2 ? yes
  i=2  1 > 2 ? NO   -> return false

opts: It returns the wrong value for empty arrays
It never stops early, and the callback does not get the index, array or thisArg
why: forEach cannot break, so it keeps calling the callback after the answer is known. That wastes work and runs side effects too often.
The real some calls cb(element, index, array) with this set to thisArg.
[1, , 3] has a hole at index 1. Array methods skip holes, so the callback runs for index 0 and 2 only.
Use i in arr to detect a hole: it is false for an empty slot.

problems.pseudo:
mySome(cb, thisArg):
  if cb is not a function -> throw TypeError
  for i from 0 to length - 1:
    if i is not in the array -> skip (hole)
    if cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this) is truthy -> return true
  return false

myEvery(cb, thisArg):
  same checks and loop
    if the call is falsy -> return false
  return true

Array.prototype.myMap = function (cb) {
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) this[i] = cb(this[i], i, this)
  return this
}

It changes the original array and returns it, instead of a new array
why: map must never mutate. Here the caller's array is overwritten, and a.myMap(f) === a is true.

  if cb is not a function -> throw TypeError
  result = new Array(length)          // same length, all holes
  for i from 0 to length - 1:
    if i is not in the array -> continue   (result keeps a hole)
    result[i] = cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)
  return result

what: filter returns a new array with only the elements whose callback result is truthy. The original array is untouched.
Unlike map, the result can be shorter, and it is always dense: holes in the source are skipped, so the result has no holes.

what: reduce walks the array and carries one value along, the accumulator. Each step returns the new accumulator; the last one is the result.
With an initialValue, the accumulator starts there and the loop starts at index 0. Without one, the first element becomes the accumulator and the loop starts at the next element.
Without an initial value on an empty array there is nothing to start from, so it throws a TypeError. Note: passing undefined explicitly still counts as "given", so you must look at arguments.length.

steps: Throw a TypeError if the callback is not a function.
If arguments.length >= 2, start with acc = initialValue and i = 0.
Otherwise find the first index that is not a hole, use that element as acc, and start after it. If there is none, throw a TypeError.
For each remaining non-hole index: acc = cb(acc, el, i, arr).
Return acc.

what: flat(depth) returns a new array where nested arrays are opened up, depth levels deep (default 1). flat(Infinity) opens everything.
flatMap(cb) is map followed by flat(1), in one pass: each callback may return an array, and its items are spread into the result.
Both skip holes, and only real arrays are opened: strings and array-like objects stay as single items.

steps: myFlat: create a result array and a recursive helper walk(list, d).
For each non-hole item: if it is an array and d > 0, call walk(item, d - 1); otherwise push the item.
Start with walk(this, depth) and return the result. Treat a missing depth as 1.
myFlatMap: for each non-hole index, call cb.call(thisArg, el, i, arr); if the value is an array, push its items, else push the value.
how.diagram:
[1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat(2)
  1          -> push 1
  [2, [3,[4]]]  depth 2 -> open
    2        -> push 2
    [3,[4]]  depth 1 -> open
      3      -> push 3
      [4]    depth 0 -> push the array itself
result: [1, 2, 3, [4]]

where: Pages of results [[...], [...]] into one list.
Deep cloning: flat copies the structure only one way, and objects stay shared.

why: The default depth is 1, so only the first level of nesting is opened.
flat(Infinity) would give [1,2,3,4].
flatMap only flattens one level. Each callback returned [[x, x*10]], which becomes [x, x*10] in the result.
To get [1,10,2,20] the callback should return [x, x * 10] (one level of nesting).

opts: flat only opens real arrays (Array.isArray), and strings are not arrays
why: A string has a length and indexes, but it is not an array, so it is kept as one item.
Use Array.isArray(item) in your check, not item.length.
flat drops holes at every level it opens: the result is [1, 2, 3].
Holes are never visited, so nothing is pushed for them.

problems.pseudo:
myFlat(depth = 1):
  result = []
  walk(list, d):
    for each index i of list:
      if i is a hole -> continue
      item = list[i]
      if item is an array and d > 0 -> walk(item, d - 1)
      else push item
  walk(this, depth)
  return result

  for each non-hole index i:
    v = cb.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)
    if v is an array -> push all its items
    else push v

what: call and apply run a function right now with a chosen this. call takes the arguments one by one, apply takes them as an array.
The trick to build them without the built-ins: a method called as obj.fn() gets this = obj. So put the function on the object for a moment, call it, and remove it again.
Use a Symbol as the temporary key so you never overwrite or show a real property. null/undefined as thisArg mean globalThis; primitives are boxed with Object(thisArg).

steps: Throw a TypeError if this (the function being called) is not a function.
Pick the context: thisArg == null ? globalThis : Object(thisArg).
Create a unique key Symbol() and set ctx[key] = this.
Call ctx[key](...args), remember the result, delete the key (in finally, so it is removed even if the function throws).
myApply: the same, with argsArray ?? [] spread as the arguments.

  ctx = user
  user[Symbol()] = greet        // borrow
  user[Symbol()]('Hi')          // called as a method: this = user
  delete user[Symbol()]         // give it back

where: Arrow functions ignore the this you pass; call/apply only change their arguments.

why: In sloppy mode, primitive this values are boxed into objects (Number, String).

think.q:
Function.prototype.myCall = function (ctx, ...args) {
  ctx.fn = this
  const r = ctx.fn(...args)
  delete ctx.fn
  return r
}
Which call breaks?
opts: f.myCall(obj) where obj already has a property fn, or f.myCall(null)
why: A fixed name like fn can overwrite (and then delete) a real property of the object. A Symbol key cannot clash.
null has no properties at all, so it must fall back to globalThis.

think.q: Why delete the temporary key inside finally?
opts: If the function throws, the key would otherwise stay on the object forever
finally is required for return values
why: Code after a throwing call never runs. finally always runs, so the object is always cleaned up.
The error still propagates to the caller, as it should.

problems.pseudo:
myCall(thisArg, ...args):
  fn = this
  if fn is not a function -> throw TypeError
  ctx = (thisArg is null or undefined) ? globalThis : Object(thisArg)
  key = new Symbol
  ctx[key] = fn
  try:
    return ctx[key](...args)      // called as a method -> this = ctx
  finally:
    delete ctx[key]

myApply(thisArg, argsArray):
  return this.myCall(thisArg, ...(argsArray or []))

what: trim removes whitespace from both ends of a string. trimStart removes it only at the start, trimEnd only at the end. Spaces in the middle stay.

myTrimStart():
  i = 0
  while i < length and isSpace(this[i]): i++
  return slice(i)

myTrimEnd():
  j = length - 1
  while j >= 0 and isSpace(this[j]): j--
  return slice(0, j + 1)

myTrim():
  return myTrimEnd of (myTrimStart of this)

what: sort orders the array in place and returns the same array. Without a compare function it turns elements into strings and compares those, so [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9].

what: Promise.resolve(value) turns any value into a promise. If the value is already a real promise, you get that same promise back. If it is a thenable (any object with a then method), it is unwrapped: the new promise follows it.
Promise.reject(reason) always returns a new rejected promise. It does not unwrap: if the reason is a promise, that promise itself becomes the rejection reason.
They are the "on-ramps" to promise land: an API can always say return Promise.resolve(cache.get(key)) and callers can always .then.

Otherwise return new Promise((res, rej) => …).
Inside: if the value is an object or function with a then method, call value.then(res, rej), so the new promise follows it. Otherwise res(value).
If reading or calling then throws, reject with that error.
myReject: return new Promise((_, rej) => rej(reason)), nothing else.

myReject(p)               -> new promise rejected WITH p as the reason

checks.t: Thenables are followed, both ways
checks.test: Promise.myResolve({ then(ok) { ok('yes') } }).then(console.log) // expected: yes
checks.verify: assert(await Promise.myResolve({ then(ok) { ok('yes') } }) === 'yes', 'should follow a fulfilling thenable'); let e; try { await Promise.myResolve({ then(_, no) { no('bad') } }) } catch (x) { e = x } assert(e === 'bad', 'should follow a rejecting thenable')
checks.gap: If value.then is a function, call value.then(res, rej) inside the executor.

checks.t: A throwing then makes the promise reject
checks.test: Promise.myResolve({ then() { throw new Error('boom') } }).catch(e => console.log(e.message)) // expected: boom
checks.verify: let msg; try { await Promise.myResolve({ then() { throw new Error('boom') } }) } catch (e) { msg = e.message } assert(msg === 'boom', 'should reject with the thrown error')
checks.gap: Wrap the thenable handling in try / catch and call rej(err).

checks.t: myReject rejects with the exact reason, never unwrapping
checks.test:
const inner = Promise.resolve(5)
Promise.myReject(inner).catch(e => console.log(e === inner)) // expected: true
checks.verify: const inner = Promise.resolve(5); const r = Promise.myReject(inner); assert(r instanceof Promise && r !== inner, 'must be a new promise'); let got; try { await r } catch (e) { got = e } assert(got === inner, 'reason must be the promise itself'); let m; try { await Promise.myReject('x') } catch (e) { m = e } assert(m === 'x', 'plain reason')
checks.gap: myReject is one line: new Promise((_, rej) => rej(reason)). Do not check for thenables.

notes: Real promise → same object. Thenable → followed. Anything else → wrapped.
Read then once and call it with this = value; reading a getter twice could give different results.
The executor's resolve/reject work only once, so a badly-behaved thenable cannot settle twice.
reject deliberately does not unwrap: a rejection reason is data, not something to follow.

what: reduceRight is reduce walking from the last element to the first. Everything else is the same: an accumulator, an optional initial value, and a TypeError for an empty array without one.
Without an initial value, the last element becomes the accumulator and the loop starts at the one before it.
It matters when the order of combining matters: building a string, nesting function calls (compose), or folding a list from the end.

steps: Throw a TypeError if the callback is not a function.
Start i at length - 1.
If an initial value was passed (arguments.length >= 2), use it. Otherwise move i down past holes, take this[i] as the accumulator and step down once more; throw if there was nothing.
While i >= 0: if index i is not a hole, acc = cb(acc, this[i], i, this); then i--.
Return acc.
how.diagram:
['a', 'b', 'c'].reduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x)
  acc = 'c' (last element), start at index 1
  i=1  'c' + 'b' = 'cb'
  i=0  'cb' + 'a' = 'cba'

where: Wrap handlers from the inside out (Redux applyMiddleware).
Building nested structures from the end of a list.
For sums and counts the direction does not matter; plain reduce reads better.

why: The last element (3) is the start, then 2, then 1.
There is no leading - because no initial value was given.

think.q:
const compose = (...fns) => (x) => fns.reduceRight((v, f) => f(v), x)
const add1 = (n) => n + 1
const double = (n) => n * 2
console.log(compose(add1, double)(5))
why: compose runs the last function first: double(5) = 10, then add1(10) = 11.
With reduce (left to right) it would be double(add1(5)) = 12.

opts: It reverses the caller's array in place, and the callback gets the wrong indexes
reduce cannot take an initial value
Nothing, it is a valid shortcut
why: reverse() mutates. After one call the original array is backwards.
Indexes are also flipped: the callback sees 0 for the real last element.
[3] is concatenated first, then [1, 2].
Inner arrays keep their own order; only the outer walk is reversed.

watch: Where does the loop start, and where does it stop?
Without an initial value, which element starts?
Does your version change the original array?

reqs: Walk from the last index down to 0; the callback gets (acc, element, index, array).
With an initial value, start from it; without one, the last real element starts.
Empty array and no initial value: throw a TypeError.
Skip holes, and do not change the original array.

checks.t: Walks from right to left
checks.test: console.log(['a', 'b', 'c'].myReduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x, '')) // expected: cba
checks.verify: assert(['a', 'b', 'c'].myReduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x, '') === 'cba', 'got ' + ['a', 'b', 'c'].myReduceRight((acc, x) => acc + x, ''))
checks.gap: Loop with i = length - 1 down to 0.

checks.t: Without an initial value the last element starts
checks.test:
let n = 0
console.log([1, 2, 3].myReduceRight((acc, x) => { n++; return acc + '-' + x }), n) // expected: 3-2-1 2
checks.verify: let n = 0; const r = [1, 2, 3].myReduceRight((acc, x) => { n++; return acc + '-' + x }); assert(r === '3-2-1', 'got ' + r); assert(n === 2, 'callback ran ' + n + ' times')
checks.gap: Take this[length - 1] as the accumulator, then start at length - 2.

checks.t: Indexes are the real positions
checks.test: console.log(['x', 'y'].myReduceRight((acc, v, i, arr) => acc + i + arr.length, '')) // expected: 1202
checks.verify: const r = ['x', 'y'].myReduceRight((acc, v, i, arr) => acc + i + arr.length, ''); assert(r === '1202', 'got ' + r)
checks.gap: Pass the real index i and the original array, not a reversed copy.

checks.t: Empty array: throws without init, returns init with one
checks.test: try { [].myReduceRight((a, b) => a) } catch (e) { console.log(e instanceof TypeError) } // expected: true
checks.verify: let ok = false; try { [].myReduceRight((a, b) => a) } catch (e) { ok = e instanceof TypeError } assert(ok, 'must throw TypeError'); assert([].myReduceRight((a) => a, 'z') === 'z', 'should return the initial value')
checks.gap: If no initial value and no real element is found, throw a TypeError.

checks.t: The original array is unchanged; holes skipped
checks.test:
const a = [1, , 3]
console.log(a.myReduceRight((s, x) => s + x), a) // expected: 4 [1, <1 empty item>, 3]
checks.verify: const a = [1, , 3]; const r = a.myReduceRight((s, x) => s + x); assert(r === 4, 'got ' + r); assert(a[0] === 1 && a[2] === 3 && !(1 in a), 'the array was changed'); const b = [, , 9]; assert(b.myReduceRight((s, x) => s + x) === 9, 'single real element')
checks.gap: Never call reverse() on this; skip holes with i in this.

notes: Same shape as reduce, mirrored: start at the end, step down.
Use arguments.length to know whether an initial value was passed.
Never use reverse() on the caller's array: it mutates and breaks the indexes.
compose is the classic real use of reduceRight.
